title: India's Chip Ambitions Take Shape as Tata and ASML Break Ground on $11 Billion Fab
excerpt: A landmark partnership between Tata Electronics and Dutch lithography giant ASML marks India's most concrete step yet towards semiconductor self-sufficiency, with the country's first commercial 300mm fab set to produce 3 billion chips annually in Gujarat.
body:
India has talked about making its own semiconductors for the better part of two decades. With the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Tata Electronics and ASML—the Dutch company that holds a near-monopoly on the lithography machines essential to chipmaking—the talk has, at last, acquired the unmistakable ring of serious intent.

The partnership centres on the construction of India's first commercial 300mm semiconductor fabrication facility in Dholera, Gujarat, backed by an investment of $11 billion (approximately ₹91,000 crore). When operational, the fab is expected to produce 50,000 wafers per month, translating to roughly 3 billion chips per year—a volume that would make a meaningful dent in India's overwhelming dependence on imported semiconductors.

## A constellation of partners

Tata and ASML are not going it alone. The project has assembled a formidable roster of technology partners. Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation (PSMC) brings decades of foundry expertise and will assist with process technology and operational know-how. Synopsys, the American electronic-design-automation giant, will provide the design tools that chip architects use to translate concepts into silicon. Merck, the German chemicals and materials group, will supply the speciality chemicals and gases without which no fab can function.

ASML's contribution is particularly significant. The company will supply deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems—the machines that etch circuit patterns onto silicon wafers with nanometre-scale precision. While these are not the most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) systems used for cutting-edge nodes below 7nm, they are the workhorses of mature-node manufacturing, perfectly suited to the 28nm to 110nm range that the Dholera fab will target.

## The right nodes for the right market

The choice of process nodes is strategically astute. While headlines tend to fixate on the race to 3nm and 2nm chips that power the latest smartphones and AI accelerators, the global economy runs on mature-node semiconductors. Automotive electronics, industrial controllers, power-management chips, display drivers, and the vast majority of Internet of Things devices all rely on chips manufactured at 28nm and above.

This is precisely the segment where supply disruptions during the pandemic caused the most widespread economic damage—and where demand continues to grow robustly. By targeting this range, the Dholera fab positions itself to serve markets where India already has significant domestic consumption: automotive (India is the world's third-largest car market), mobile handsets, and the rapidly expanding digital-infrastructure buildout.

## Government backing and economics

The Indian government is underwriting approximately 70 per cent of the project cost through its India Semiconductor Mission, reflecting the strategic priority accorded to chip manufacturing. The remaining capital comes from Tata and its partners. First chips are expected to roll off the line in late 2026, an ambitious timeline that will test the ability of Indian infrastructure to support the exacting requirements of semiconductor fabrication—including ultra-pure water supply, uninterrupted power, and vibration-free environments.

The facility is projected to generate more than 20,000 direct and indirect jobs, creating an ecosystem of suppliers, technicians, and engineers in what is currently a largely agricultural region of Gujarat.

## What it means for the diaspora

For the substantial Indian-origin workforce in the global semiconductor industry—engineers at TSMC, Intel, Samsung, and scores of fabless design houses—the Dholera project represents a potential new career vector. Industry observers expect Tata to recruit aggressively among the diaspora, particularly those with foundry-operations experience.

The geopolitical implications are equally significant. As nations scramble to reduce their dependence on Taiwan and China for chip supply, India's entry into mature-node manufacturing adds a new node—if readers will forgive the pun—to the global supply network. For Indian industry, which currently imports nearly all of its semiconductors, domestic production promises both supply security and, eventually, cost advantages.

## The road ahead

Sceptics will note that India has announced semiconductor ambitions before, only to see them founder on execution challenges. The Dholera project is different in one crucial respect: it has committed capital, named technology partners, and a customer base that is largely domestic and growing. Whether it can meet its late-2026 target for first silicon will be the first real test of India's chipmaking resolve.
